Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Strait of Hormuz Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reach Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile Guardian staff and agencies Sat 8 Aug 2026 17.01 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 20.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday. Iran’s politburo-like body known as the supreme national security council said the strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, and its state broadcaster published a statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets. Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war Read more There was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets. The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation , “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening is contingent on other conditions, he said, in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal. Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the talks, said in a statement on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait. Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, repeatedly attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route. The US opposes any Iranian tolls in the strait, though the June deal allows Tehran to hammer out arrangements for the “future administration” of Hormuz in conjunction with fellow coastal state Oman. The 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended. Iran has said it was close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries. Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement. “There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying. Continued attacks in the strait, which was free to sail through before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have since urged both sides to return to the terms of the June memorandum. The strait, which is crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low. Meanwhile, a vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned Adnoc oil and gas company was attacked while sailing through the strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said earlier on Saturday. The foreign ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping. Adnoc said in a statement that there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday. The company said more than a dozen of its vessels have been attacked by missiles and drones while using the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member has been killed and 20 others wounded, it said. Adnoc did not elaborate on the location of the attack or any damage. Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, and the vessel and crew were safe. It was not clear whether this was the Adnoc incident. https://kelo.com/2026/08/05/albanian-fir.text: Sign In Search News Weather Shows Blogs Podcasts More Contests Events Pictures Austria hits record temperature, Hungary curbs power use as Europe feels the heat By Thomson Reuters Aug 5, 2026 | 5:45 AM By Krisztina Than and Florion Goga BUDAPEST/MALLAKASTER, Albania, Aug 5 (Reuters) – The temperature in Austria climbed to a record high on Wednesday, while Hungarians curbed power use as the latest heatwave and drought took their toll on central and southern Europe. Europe, the world’s fastest warming continent, has been ravaged by record-breaking heat and ​destructive wildfires this summer, with France and Spain particularly hard hit in recent weeks. The focus of the ‌heatwave has shifted further east, with Italy placing its major cities under a red heat alert as temperatures climbed to around 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in some areas. In Albania, emergency services battled a wildfire in the southern region of Mallakaster. The heat prompted the Vatican to move Pope Leo’s first weekly general audience after the July break indoors rather than hold it in St. Peter’s Square. Visitors to Rome welcomed the ‌decision ​as they sought relief from the sweltering conditions. “I suppose it’s better to hold ⁠it indoors because of the heat,” a ⁠tourist from Mexico, Diego Amaya, said. AUSTRIA HAS RECORD HIGH AGAIN The temperature hit a record 41.2 C (106.2 Fahrenheit) in the Austrian town of Bad Deutsch-Altenburg near the border with Slovakia, national weather service GeoSphere Austria said. The previous record of 41.0 C was set on Tuesday in nearby Vienna. Across the border in Hungary, companies and households cut power ​consumption this week after a government appeal to ease pressure on the grid amid the severe drought. The capital Budapest is facing the peak of the heatwave over the next two days, with temperatures rising close to 40 C on ⁠Wednesday afternoon. Dwindling water levels on the Danube have forced Hungary to ⁠largely shut down its sole nuclear plant, which uses the river’s waters for cooling, creating an ​energy crisis that has stretched power supply capacity to its limits. Slovenia’s only nuclear power plant, Krsko, which supplies neighbouring Croatia as ​well, said on Wednesday it would begin reducing reactor output overnight due to exceptionally high temperatures ‌and low flows on the Sava River, which flows into the Danube. The plant will initially cut generation to 80% of capacity. Further west, water levels on the river Rhine in Germany have hit new lows, with some cargo services stopping and other sailings continuing but with greatly reduced loads. The Rhine is a route for commodities including grains, ores and petrol. WILDFIRES BURN ⁠IN ALBANIA In Albania’s southern Mallakaster region, wildfires forced the evacuation of about 15 families along with their livestock and pets, while ground and aerial crews fought to stop the flames reaching homes near a village. Efforts continued to tame another wildfire, likely caused ⁠by lightning, in rocky, mountainous terrain south ‌of the Albanian city of Gjirokaster. In neighbouring Greece, a wildfire, possibly caused by vibrating ⁠electricity conductors and fanned by gale-force winds, has burned thousands of hectares of farmland near ​a popular ‌holiday destination northwest of Athens. The blaze appeared largely contained on Wednesday, but hundreds of ​firefighters remained in ⁠the area to prevent flare-ups as six helicopters doused scattered smoking spots. The hot, dry summer is having a worrying impact on agriculture. Britain’s cereal harvest is on track to be the worst since comparable records began in 1984, according to an analysis published on Wednesday, as crops wither after one of the driest and hottest spring-summer periods on record. (Reporting by Francois Murphy, Florion Goga, Krisztina Than, Veronica Altimari, Matteo Negri, Ivana Sekularac and Michael Hogan; Writing by Angeliki Koutantou and Keith Weir; Editing by Mark Potter, ​Alex Richardson and Ros Russell) Comments Leave a Reply Cancel reply You must be logged in to post a comment. https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/noomi-r.text: By Joe George | August 19, 2026 | Share on Facebook (opens in a new tab) Share on X (opens in a new tab) Share on Linkedin (opens in a new tab) Share on email (opens in a new tab) | Comments count: 0 Photo: Focus Features Hot Spot isn’t an easy movie. Directed by Polish auteur Agnieszka Smoczyńska—best known for The Lure , a horror/musical take on The Little Mermaid — Hot Spot explores pressing issues like AI, state surveillance, police violence, and immigration. But it does so through a surreal, sci-fi lens, one that takes time out for ecstatic dance sequences and animal transformations. Hot Spot may baffle as many viewers as it thrills, but that’s nothing new for star Noomi Rapace . After all, she was in Prometheus , the highly-anticipated Alien prequel that turned out to be a mediation on humanity’s relationship to God. “I love Prometheus . I think Prometheus is a masterpiece,” Rapace declares to Den of Geek . “ Ridley Scott is a genius, and it was an amazing experience for me. Some movies I’ve done are not masterpieces, and they still do really well. I’ll hear something I’ve done is number one on Netflix, and I’ll think, ‘Oh, my god!'” she jokes. “But, what’s beautiful with films and storytelling is that something like Prometheus can find a new audience 10, 20, 30 years later.” A Rebel in an Artificial World Such knowledge gives Rapace the confidence to work on a bold project like Hot Spot . Set in the near future, Hot Spot stars Andrzej Konopka as Jan 623, a detective who works for the Head, the AI system that controls every part of human life. Jan’s job sometimes exposes him to the worst parts of humanity, but he considers the toll worthwhile if it makes things safe for his wife, musician Ayka (Reika Kirishima), and their son Zen (George Aurimas Cris). But when a brutal murder brings him in contact with the mysterious Rana (Rapace), Jan must face truths about society he’d rather ignore. “Rana is a cyber witch, she calls herself a witch,” explains Rapace of her character. “She doesn’t want to be cyber witch, but she’s lived through a lot of trauma and experienced a lot of violence and chaos. She’s traveled from country to country because she’s had to keep moving throughout life. Ad Ad – content continues below “She’s used to battlefields, but, when we meet her in the movie, she’s a voice of love and peace. She leads a group called the Neo-Souls, but she doesn’t want to see herself as a leader because she sees the group as a community, a collective. The Neo-Souls move in peace in a world where the only crime they commit is refusing to be hooked up to Big AI, to the Head. They don’t carry passports, they don’t have an identity that belongs to a country or a regime or a religion. They just move and walk through the world, praying and preaching love.” For as peaceful as Rana may be, the experience of playing her has forced Rapace to confront a very different aspect of herself. “I’ve been thinking about my own rage,” she admits. “I grew up being angry at the world, at injustice and racism. This movie makes me think I want to change my approach. I’ve tried being angry and shouting and fighting, and it’s obviously not working because there are always people who are louder or crazier or more violent. That way is not working. “So we need to find a way in this crazy world right now to meet people with empathy, with curiosity, to try to listen. I need to find a way to speak my truth but not force it upon people.” Those questions only become more pressing when Rapace faces something like AI, a major element in Hot Spot . “We have to think about who we are and what we are,” she insists. “We’re so attached to technology and our phones. My phone is in my hand all the time, or it least it was. But I had to ask myself, ‘What about hearing your own thoughts? What about being on your own or being bored? What happens then?’ “So, I’ve been reflecting on my own behavior, and that of people around me. It’s made space for loads of conversations with really interesting people.” Unfamiliar Forms Although Hot Spot can create the type of change that Rapace has already integrated into her own life, she also acknowledges that such a weird, surrealistic movie can elicit a whole range of emotions. Structurally, Hot Spot follows the beats of a police procedural, in which the detective Jan learns about a crime and begins questioning suspects, including Rana. That familiar format could lend itself to misunderstandings, and Rapace is okay with that. Ad Ad – content continues below “ Hot Spot’ s a fun ride. And it’s a fantasy, a fairy-tale for adults,” she says. “Viewers can enter the movie through its humor and madness, because it’s a trip. It’s not the type of movie where you go in to understand everything. You can’t demand to know the narrative and have clear understanding of what happens at the end of each act. Join our mailing list Get the best of Den of Geek delivered right to your inbox! Rapace insists, “I trust the audience. I think the audience is really smart. The audience is used to being force-fed very simple premises with no loose ends, but I think they get bored easily. After twenty minutes, they realize they know what’s going to happen next. So when something’s new, they’re like, ‘Okay, wow!’ “My son has seen the Hot Spot trailer a couple of times, and he’s been asking a lot of questions. He’s curious, because he plays a lot of games and kids, young adults, they live in a different reality where there is no straight narrative. They have visuals and events and lots of things happening. But they don’t think it’s too much. They keep moving, they go with the flow. “I think that makes for a different way to watch a movie. You should just allow yourself to go on a journey and maybe not think so much. Hopefully, some emotions will come up that you can deal with or understand later, rather than trying to be rational and put the pieces together to understand it.” Rapace knows the value of going on a journey with Hot Spot because she’s already done it, going back to when she first received the script, credited to Robert Bolesto. “ Hot Spot ‘s not a normal movie,” she says. “Even when I read this script, I kept asking, ‘Wait, what? What’s going on?’ The script was only 65 pages, instead of 90 to 130 pages. But Agnieszka worked with the environment to give it voice and character. The place where we shot tells me about the time, and it almost feels like dancing to make the movie. Ad Ad – content continues below “The madness and the humor drew me to the project. It’s dystopian, neo-punk and rebellious. It’s wild. But it’s not pointing fingers at you. It’s just asking you to think about your life, and reflect a little bit about who you want to be, to what extent you want to be hooked up and connected. How much of your own freedom and privacy are you ready to sacrifice? “The movie’s throwing out those questions, but it’s not telling the audience to do this or that.” Navigating the New By Reconsidering the Old Which is exactly what Rapace wants in a film role. “I’m looking for complexity,” she points out. “I want something that connects with the questions I’m asking myself and thinking about, something that hooks into me.” “Sometimes, that’s the director. Agnieszka Smoczyńska is brilliant as a person, a woman, an artist. She’s so brave and curious and strong. I was obsessed with The Lure , because it’s so sexy and strange. So getting a chance to work with Agnieszka, and go on a journey to her was a big draw to Hot Spot .” Of course, Rapace also had some guidance in the form of the characters she played in the past, which informed her take on Rana. “Rana’s got a little bit of Lisbeth Salander from The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo , because she’s an outsider going up against the system, particularly a system run by computer. She’s also Elizabeth Shaw from Prometheus , asking questions about who we are and the nature of truth. There’s even a bit of Mother Teresa, who I played in Mother (2025, directed by Teona Strugar Mitevska), asking if I’m good or bad. “Rana is a cocktail of different characters that I’ve played before. And she’s a lot of me, because she’s someone who keeps moving and keeps asking herself questions to evolve and deal with things in a new way.” Ad Ad – content continues below And in that way, Rana is like us filmgoers too, because we too are always evolving—whether that’s finding new ways of engaging with films, new challenges in the world in which we live, or simply reconsidering films that may have disappointed us a decade and a half ago to realize that, yes, Prometheus is a masterpiece. Hot Spot releases to theaters on August 21, 2026. https://voiceofvienna.org/macron-warns-o.text: French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that Russia’s hybrid campaign against Europe and France is growing more intense, prompting Paris to draw up emergency plans to shield critical infrastructure and defence sites from attack, according to BBC News. Speaking at the Élysée Palace after talks with party leaders on the security fallout from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, Macron said France had already been hit by Russian hybrid operations in recent weeks and would not respond “without a response”. He pointed to last month’s drone strike on Leipzig airport in Germany, widely blamed on Moscow, and to warnings from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk that Russia may be planning drone and missile strikes against NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank. “In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified,” Macron said. “The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite.” Hybrid attacks, a loose term covering cyber intrusions, sabotage, disinformation and other non military pressure are often carried out through proxies, with Russia routinely denying involvement even as evidence mounts. Across Europe, officials have reported suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, some openly attributed to Moscow. Tusk told Polish lawmakers there was a “real risk” of strikes on NATO soil, with Russia potentially claiming they were “accidental” to sow division inside the alliance. Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine–Poland border minutes after former British prime minister Boris Johnson and senior European security officials had travelled along the same line; all passengers were evacuated before the engine was struck. While President Vladimir Putin insists Russia does not plan to attack Europe, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has warned that sending troops to Ukraine would be seen as a declaration of war, promising a “completely different” and “very short” conflict. Moscow has also reiterated that any British military facilities in Ukraine used to strike Russian territory are “legitimate targets”. Macron said France would convene a G7 meeting on energy security and discuss gas stocks with the European Commission, including possible releases of strategic reserves. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Isabella Stasiak’s parents were known to social services and the police, the court was told Photograph: Warwickshire police Isabella Stasiak’s parents were known to social services and the police, the court was told Photograph: Warwickshire police UK news Parents inflicted fatal physical and sexual abuse on their baby, Warwick court hears Michal Stasiak and Kinga Wydrzynska pleaded not guilty to 11 counts relating to death of 13-month-old Isabella Stasiak Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.05 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 13-month-old girl was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of her parents before she was fatally injured by her mother, a court has heard. Michal Stasiak, 28, and Kinga Wydrzynska, 26, appeared at Warwick crown court on Tuesday, where they pleaded not guilty to 11 counts related to the death of Isabella Stasiak. Wydrzynska is charged with Isabella’s murder, while both parents have been charged with one count of causing or allowing the death of a child, four counts of causing or allowing serious physical harm to a child, two counts related to the sexual assault of a child and three counts of child cruelty. The court heard both parents were known to social services and the police. Isabella died in hospital after sustaining a series of injuries including a fractured skull and ribs, a broken arm and a burn to her entire face, the court was told. In her opening statement to the court on Tuesday, Annabel Darlow KC said emergency services were called to the Wydrzynska’s home in the early hours of 7 January 2025 where Isabella was found “grey and lifeless”. Medical experts later concluded Isabella died “because she suffered injuries consistent with a forceful direct impact to her head against a hard surface”, Darlow told the court. Darlow said Wydrzynska was the only adult present at the home when Isabella was found by police and the injuries were the “devastating culmination of systematic physical abuse”. “The prosecution say, by the time Isabella died, there was an entrenched pattern of abuse, neglect and mistreatment of the little girl of which both parents were entirely aware,” Darlow told the court. “Before she died, Isabella was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of both her mother and father,” Darlow added. “Neither defendant has ever provided any explanation for those injuries to their daughter.” Jurors were told Isabella was born in December 2023 and immediately taken into the care of social services. After being placed in emergency accommodation, Isabella was looked after by foster parents for four months before she was returned to her parents in April 2024 – nine months before her death, the court was told. Members of the jury were also told Stasiak was arrested by police for common assault after a report was made by Wydrzynska on 14 December 2024, less than a month before Isabella’s death. Wydrzynska made repeated attempts to withdraw the report, jurors were told. However, Stasiak was placed on police bail and prohibited from living at the family home or contacting Wydrzynska. In addition, the court was told police officers had attended the family home after a complaint was made by a neighbour in October 2024. Officers attended the property and were only responded to when the police threatened to force entry, Darlow said. Officers spoke to the parents and saw Isabella and “did not have any immediate safeguarding concerns” after the visit, the court was told. The trial continues.
